text: This lesson is about REF CURSORs, and it starts from a problem you've probably never had to think about in T-SQL. In T-SQL, a bare select inside a stored procedure just streams its result set straight back to whoever called it. You've never had to do anything special for that to work.

Oracle procedures don't behave that way. A select by itself inside a PL-SQL procedure has nowhere to go. Ordinary cursors, from Lesson 31, let you process a result set row by row inside PL-SQL, but that's not the same as handing a result set back out to the caller. A REF CURSOR is Oracle's answer: a cursor variable, opened for a query at runtime with open for, instead of a fixed query declared up front.

And here's how it actually solves the original problem: give a procedure an out parameter typed sys ref cursor, open that parameter for the query inside the procedure body, and the caller — another PL-SQL block, or an application using an Oracle driver — receives a live, open cursor it can fetch rows from. This is the real, explicit equivalent of what T-SQL hands you for free.

Sys ref cursor is the generic, weakly typed ref cursor type most developers reach for, because it can be opened for any query shape at all, which is exactly what makes it flexible enough to declare once and pass around through procedure calls.

And because it's a variable, not a fixed declaration, the same REF CURSOR can be opened for entirely different queries depending on runtime logic — an if branch opening one query, an else branch opening another — something an ordinary named cursor, whose query is fixed at declaration time, simply cannot do.

Next lesson: PL-SQL collections — VARRAYs, nested tables, and associative arrays, the three real in-memory collection types PL-SQL gives you that T-SQL's table variables and temp tables don't quite match. See you there.
